q: The FDA warning on repeated or lengthy anaesthesia and brain development applies to:
o: Children under 3 and 2nd-trimester pregnancy
Children under 3 years, but not pregnancy
Children under 2 and 3rd-trimester pregnancy
Under 3 years, and 3rd-trimester pregnancy
e: Families should be told what is known and what studies are under way so consent is fully informed. Anaesthesia risks include nausea, vomiting, bronchospasm, laryngospasm, stridor, emergence delirium and maladaptive behaviour afterwards.

q: Which statement about pain in children is FALSE?
o: Self-report is the gold standard for assessment
Preoperative anxiety predicts postoperative pain
Self-report scales cannot be used under 2 years
Discussing expectations changes procedural pain
e: Book answer: the statement that self-assessment scales are 'not present' under 2 years is the false one (observational scales such as PIPP exist for premature infants, neonates and non-verbal or impaired children). Validated self-report tools: Pieces of Hurt (3–6 years), Faces and Oucher (4–12), VAS (8–16). Describe pain by intensity, location, duration, quality and what modifies it. Child life specialists reduce child and parental anxiety. Use multimodal analgesia, and dispose of unused opioids properly.

q: Which paediatric fasting (NPO) interval is correct?
o: Full meal: 6 hours
Formula milk: 4 hours
Clear fluids: 2 hours
Breast milk: 6 hours
e: Full or fatty meal (including enteral feeds) 8 h; formula, non-human milk or light meal 6 h; breast milk 4 h; clear liquids 2 h. NPO violation raises the risk of aspiration and pneumonitis.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Give antiseizure, reflux and asthma drugs that morning
Stop metformin 24 h before because of lactic acidosis
Fasting diabetics are mainly at risk of hypoglycaemia
Children on a ketogenic diet get carbohydrate-free fluids
e: Per the book, volume depletion during fasting plus stopping diabetic drugs leads to hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia, so this is the false statement. Enteral feeds count as a fatty meal (stop 8 h before).

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Routine laboratory tests have little value
Pregnancy testing is advised in girls of childbearing age
Elective opening of the urinary tract is clean-contaminated
The AAP advises a routine preoperative chest X-ray
e: Routine tests (including chest X-ray) are not recommended. Obtain urine cultures when indicated and treat positive cultures by sensitivity; recurrent preoperative UTI is a high-risk factor for postoperative infection. AUA: if surgery proceeds despite infection, give antibiotics to sterilise the field.

q: Which statement about premature infants is FALSE?
o: Aim for an oxygen saturation of 98–100%
They have a high risk of apnoea, which can be fatal
They lose fluid quickly from skin and wounds
They cannot concentrate their urine well
e: Supplemental oxygen raises the risk of retinopathy and blindness, so aim for saturations in the low 90s. Lung problems: low surfactant (especially <36 weeks), high oxygen consumption, low FRC and tracheomalacia. Perioperative complications are much more frequent, mostly in the immediate postoperative period.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: High FiO2 after bleomycin can cause fatal lung toxicity
Raised urea causes platelet dysfunction and thrombosis
Dehydration is the key perioperative issue in sickle cell
CKD anaemia reflects low erythropoietin and high urea
e: Uraemia impairs platelets, raising bleeding (not thrombosis) risk. Under-6 CKD is mostly congenital (not acquired IgA nephropathy); cardiac function is often abnormal; electrolyte disturbance (e.g. hyperkalaemia) causes arrhythmias. CKD stage 2 needs no dose changes, but watch NSAIDs.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Latex anaphylaxis causes bronchospasm and hypotension
Spina bifida raises the risk of latex allergy
Spina bifida T5–T8 lesions can cause dysreflexia
CAH causes adrenaline excess and hyperglycaemia
e: CAH can cause adrenaline and cortisol deficiency, leading to hypoglycaemia. Autonomic dysreflexia (classically injury at or above T6; the book cites T5–T8 lesions) gives severe hypertension, bradycardia, stroke and possible death; know its signs. Severe latex reaction: bronchoconstriction, vasodilatation and hypotension, capillary leak, coronary vasoconstriction and myocardial depression. Spina bifida brings multiple comorbidities.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Perioperative fever is rarely due to infection
Nerve blocks are unsafe in any septic child
After a URTI, airways stay reactive 2–8 weeks
Trauma patients have an empty stomach if fasted 6 h
e: Commonest perioperative fever cause: infection, usually viral URTI. Transfusion can cause non-specific fever up to a week later. Treat every trauma child as having a full stomach (rapid sequence induction). In sepsis, peripheral nerve blocks avoid systemic opioid effects. Antibiotics are the mainstay of sepsis treatment: give early and culture if possible.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: ERAS components are well proven in children
Anaphylaxis: stop drug, oxygen, fluids, adrenaline
Muscle relaxants and beta-lactams are main triggers
Give antibiotics early enough for tissue levels
e: ERAS (avoid long fasting, early feeding, carbohydrate loading, early mobilisation, education) is yet to be established in children. Anaphylaxis treatment also includes Trendelenburg position. Antibiotic choice depends on site and likely source.

q: Which statement about malignant hyperthermia is TRUE?
o: Late: metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia
Early signs: hypocarbia and sinus bradycardia
Stop trigger, call help, swap machine, A-line
It is common and triggered by acetylcholine
e: MH is rare, potentially fatal and hypermetabolic, triggered by volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine (the book's option says 'acetylcholine'). Signs: hypercarbia, tachycardia, masseter spasm and hyperthermia; late: severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia, rigidity and rhabdomyolysis. Also insert a Foley catheter. The specific antidote is dantrolene (not named in the book's answer). Postoperatively, most cardiac events are preventable; high preoperative anxiety raises the risk of emergence delirium (not limited to ages 2–8); respiratory events are more than hypoxia and obstruction.

q: Which statement about cosmesis in paediatric MIS is TRUE?
o: Scars shrink as children grow taller
Scar site matters more than size
Parents value cosmesis over outcomes
Single-port benefit lasts many years
e: Validated scar questionnaires exist. Families prefer inconspicuous locations, put clinical outcomes ahead of cosmesis, and choose MIS when outcomes are equal. Single-site cosmesis is no better than standard laparoscopy at 18 months.

q: Which procedure has NOT shown a length-of-stay benefit with a minimally invasive approach?
o: Appendicovesicostomy
Ureteric reimplantation
Augmentation cystoplasty
Hernia/hydrocele repair
e: Pyeloplasty also shows benefit. Laparoscopic hernia repair may cause more pain than an open inguinal incision (pneumoperitoneum stress); MIS benefit is proportional to the burden of the open alternative.

q: Which statement about pneumoperitoneum in children is FALSE?
o: Ejection fraction is maintained as workload rises
Cardiac index falls above about 10 mmHg
Mortality is unchanged with heart defects
Insufflation may trigger vagal bradycardia
e: Mortality is higher in children with congenital heart defects, so use close monitoring and a cardiac anaesthesia team. Bradycardia responds to atropine or glycopyrrolate and is usually self-limited; sympathetic tachyarrhythmia may also occur.

q: Which change with pneumoperitoneum is described WRONGLY?
o: End-tidal CO2 increases
Systemic vascular resistance rises
Dynamic lung compliance increases
Intracranial pressure increases
e: Compliance falls (diaphragm pushed up, smaller tidal volumes), so ventilator settings often need changing. ETCO2 rises from CO2 absorption and reduced minute ventilation. Raised SVR drives a sympathetic response; GFR and urine output fall. ICP rises, usually not clinically relevant. Infants have little working space, a pliable abdominal wall and marked cardiopulmonary changes.

q: Which statement about the immune response is TRUE?
o: Peritoneal signs are sharper after laparoscopy
CRP and IL-6 are lower after laparoscopy
Room-air insufflation blunts inflammation more
Children gain more immune benefit than adults
e: CO2 insufflation blunts local and systemic inflammation compared with air or open surgery, reducing pain and fatigue but also masking peritonitis. Keep a high suspicion of visceral injury in an ill child without an acute abdomen.

q: Which is an absolute contraindication to MIS in children?
o: Intolerance of pneumoperitoneum
Age below 3 months at surgery
Previous abdominal operations
Body weight below 4 kilograms
e: The only absolute contraindications: inability to tolerate pneumoperitoneum, and the surgeon being unable to do it minimally invasively. Infants under a week old have had safe procedures. Prior surgery raises conversion risk but such children may benefit more.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Umbilical ports seldom need any fascial closure
Bifurcation lies below it in up to 40%
Trendelenburg does not alter the relationship
Umbilical fascial defects are rare in children
e: Fascial openings are common in children (and up to 25% of adults), so close umbilical ports. Trendelenburg increases the chance that the bifurcation lies below the umbilicus; blind umbilical entry risks the aorta and IVC. The vessel most often hit by an umbilical Veress needle is the left common iliac vein, the most superior vessel there, crossing the iliac artery; recognise it before dilating.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Port hernias never occur below 5 mm
Open access has more visceral injuries
Veress access fails more often than open
The umbilicus is the highest-risk hernia site
e: Major vascular or visceral injury rates are similar with either technique. Omental herniation has been reported through a 3 mm site, so close all ports in children; no location is protective (unlike adults). Hernias may present only with lethargy and a bulge because peritoneal signs are blunted.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Embolus may raise or lower end-tidal CO2
The best rescue position is prone
CO2 tubing contains only pure CO2 gas
Gas embolism is common but rarely serious
e: Up to 10% of initial gas may be nitrogen or oxygen from the tubing, so flush the tubing, especially in infants. Embolism is rare but life-threatening; place the child in left lateral decubitus. Training aids: standardised skill assessments, validated low- and high-fidelity simulation, and warm-up; there is no standardised urological curriculum across centres (FLS exists in general surgery).

q: Per the book, a paediatric uroflow is valid when the voided volume is:
o: Over 50 mL
Any volume
Over 150 mL
Over 100 mL
e: Ideally >50 mL and <115% of expected bladder capacity (larger volumes can mislead). Adults use >150 mL. Qmax is the most relevant quantitative measure. Non-invasive urodynamics: uroflowmetry, patch EMG and pelvic ultrasound.

q: The five ICCS (2014) reference uroflow curve shapes are:
o: Bell, tower, peaked, inverted, normal
Bell, tower, staccato, interrupted, flat
Bell, plateau, high, normal, staccato
Bell, peaked, stuttering, normal, plateau
e: The ICCS standardisation document (J Urol 2014) defines the terminology for voiding dysfunction and its tests.

q: Which pairing of EMG lag time and pattern is correct?
o: Over 6 s: overactive bladder and tower curve
Under 2 s: bladder neck dysfunction, plateau
Over 6 s: bladder neck dysfunction, plateau
2–6 s: overactive bladder and tower curve
e: Normal lag 2–6 s with a bell curve; <2 s overactive bladder with a tower curve; >6 s primary bladder neck dysfunction with a plateau after an initial rise. EMG also shows whether voiding is synergic or dyssynergic.

q: Which statement about bladder capacity is TRUE?
o: Functional capacity = smallest diary void
(Age + 2) × 30 mL is functional capacity
Capacity cannot be judged from a diary
Functional capacity = voided + PVR
e: Functional capacity reflects what the bladder holds day to day: uroflow voided volume plus PVR, or the largest voided volume on the diary (the book's key says 'a + d' but its text muddles this). (Age + 2) × 30 mL (Koff) estimates expected capacity over 1 year; ICCS uses (age + 1) × 30 mL.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Creatinine is needed in all LUTS children
Debris means symptomatic UTI is likely
Malodorous urine reliably predicts infection
Bladder debris predicts a positive culture
e: Interpret debris cautiously in asymptomatic children. Ultrasound also gives prevoid and postvoid volumes, wall thickness and rectal diameter. Every child with LUTS and no prior diagnosis needs a urinalysis (specific gravity, protein, glucose, WBC, RBC, bacteria). Blood tests only if upper tract disease is suspected.

q: Per the book, which sacral finding carries the highest risk of occult spinal dysraphism?
o: Simple dimple
Hair tuft
Dermal sinus
Haemangioma
e: Book order, lowest to highest: simple dimple, symmetric bifid gluteal cleft, hypertrichosis, dermal sinus, haemangioma. Examine the back (dimples, cleft deviation, hair, sinuses, vascular lesions) and palpate the sacrum.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Videourodynamics can diagnose spinal dysraphism
MRI is the gold standard; US up to 6 months
CT is the gold standard for occult dysraphism
Ultrasound is as sensitive as MRI at any age
e: For low-likelihood findings (e.g. a deviated gluteal cleft in a 6-month-old) ultrasound is reasonable; inconclusive or positive scans go to MRI.

q: A child's LUT dysfunction has failed timed voiding and avoiding irritants. Next:
o: Start an antimuscarinic
Start an alpha-blocker
Formal videourodynamics
Bowel–bladder diary
e: Diaries (7-day bowel–bladder or 48-hour frequency–volume) reveal small capacity, infrequent voiding, nocturia and polydipsia before invasive tests. Validated questionnaires: DVSS, DVISS, ISI-P (symptoms), PinQ (quality of life), CBCL and SSIPPE (behaviour).

q: LUT dysfunction in children is associated with:
o: All of these
VUR alone
Constipation alone
Recurrent UTI alone
e: Constipation, neuropsychiatric problems, UTI and VUR all associate with LUT dysfunction. History should cover symptoms, frequency, bowel function, UTIs, family, prenatal and birth history, milestones and toilet training, neuropsychiatric, medical, surgical and social history, and diet. First decide whether it is a storage or an emptying disorder.

q: The appropriate cystometry fill rate in a child is:
o: 20% of expected capacity/min
A fixed 5 mL per minute
A fixed 20 mL per minute
5–10% of expected capacity/min
e: A fixed 20 mL/min would be too fast for a neonate with an 80 mL bladder. Urodynamics is the gold standard for LUT dysfunction.

q: Which urodynamic finding is reduced when the study is done under sedation?
o: Compliance
Capacity
Overactivity
Leak point
e: Only detrusor overactivity is reliably suppressed. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis or pre-study cultures do not prevent post-study UTI (1.4%).

q: Which statement about VUR epidemiology is TRUE?
o: Inherited VUR is thought to be recessive
Black girls have more VUR than white girls
About 30% of children with UTI have VUR
About 10% of siblings of refluxers have VUR
e: About 17% without infection. About one-third of siblings have VUR; inheritance is thought autosomal dominant. Girls of African descent have about a 10-fold lower frequency; antenatally detected reflux is similar in Black and white infants.

q: Which statement about antenatally detected reflux is FALSE?
o: Renal impairment at birth reflects dysplasia
It is usually lower grade in boys than girls
It is more often bilateral in boys
It shows a clear male preponderance
e: Antenatally detected reflux in boys is usually high grade and bilateral, often with congenital dysplasia. Reflux found later in life is mostly in girls. Cardinal associated anomalies: multicystic dysplastic kidney and renal agenesis; high-grade reflux associates with renal maldevelopment.

q: Which statement about sibling reflux is FALSE?
o: Prophylaxis while deciding on screening is reasonable
Siblings under 5 with normal kidneys may skip VCUG
Once found, treatment indications differ from usual
Siblings with cortical defects have most to lose
e: Treatment indications for sibling reflux are the same as for any child with reflux. Age, UTI history and renal imaging guide whether to screen.

q: Primary reflux results from a deficiency of the:
o: Longitudinal muscle, intravesical ureter
Circular muscle, extravesical ureter
Circular muscle, intravesical ureter
Longitudinal muscle, extravesical ureter
e: Paquin found a 5:1 tunnel length to diameter ratio in normal children; aim for 5:1 at reimplantation. Mackie and Stephens: a laterally (cranially) placed bud explains primary reflux; a caudal (medial) bud tends to be obstructed.

q: Which statement about secondary reflux is TRUE?
o: Neurogenic reflux needs prompt surgery
Anatomic obstruction is common in girls
Sacral hair patches are irrelevant to VUR
Valves are the commonest obstruction
e: 48–70% of boys with valves have VUR, and relieving obstruction resolves many. In girls the commonest structural obstruction is a prolapsing ureterocele. Treat neurogenic reflux by its primary cause. Look for occult dysraphism (dimples, hair, cleft).

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Subureteric bulking agents damage the UVJ
Pressures above 40 cmH2O associate with VUR
Infection can weaken the UVJ and cause reflux
Poor compliance damages the UVJ over time
e: Bulking agents have not been shown to harm the UVJ. Poor compliance, detrusor decompensation and incomplete emptying gradually damage it. Non-neurogenic neurogenic bladder: voluntary sphincter dyssynergia with gradual decompensation and myogenic failure from residual urine. Infection lowers compliance, raises pressure and distorts the UVJ. Upper tract damage can occur below 40 cmH2O too.

q: Which statement about functional causes of reflux is FALSE?
o: Curtsying in girls is a sign of bladder dysfunction
Treatment aims to damp contractions and lower pressure
Initial management of functional reflux is medical
Urethral dilation is part of standard treatment
e: Urethral dilation has no role. Other signs: dribbling, urgency, incontinence, boys squeezing the penis. Always ask about voiding patterns. Constipation and encopresis often accompany reflux and UTI.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Dwoskin–Perlmutter is the current standard
The 1981 International system is the standard
Grading is accurate despite UPJ obstruction
A MAG3 scan grades reflux with UPJ obstruction
e: The International Reflux Study system (1981) merged Heikel–Parkkulainen (Europe) and Dwoskin–Perlmutter (USA). Accurate grading is impossible with ipsilateral obstruction. If both UPJ and UVJ need surgery, repair the UPJ first. Reflux cannot be graded accurately with posterior urethral valves either.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Fever always produces a renal scar
Fever reliably proves pyelonephritis
Fever needs over 10^5 CFU per mL
Fever raises the yield of finding VUR
e: Fever is not always reliable for upper tract involvement and can occur with <100,000 colonies. A girl with recurrent proven afebrile UTIs and a scar on DMSA warrants VCUG and ultrasound; a bagged specimen or no pyuria should make you question the UTI diagnosis; over 5 years, UTI alone does not mandate VCUG. Older girls with asymptomatic bacteriuria need no screening; focus on voiding, bowels and fluids.

q: Which statement about cystography is FALSE?
o: Some reflux appears only during infection
VCUG in active infection underestimates
Catheter or anaesthesia studies may misgrade reflux
Overhydration may mask low-grade reflux
e: During infection, endotoxins paralyse ureteric smooth muscle and exaggerate dilatation, so reflux is overestimated, not underestimated.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Ultrasound can reliably exclude reflux
Nuclear cystography gives more anatomic detail
DTPA is best for pyelonephritis and scars
Ultrasound first assesses the upper tracts
e: Kidney appearance on ultrasound does not correlate with the presence or grade of reflux. Radionuclide cystography is accurate for detection and follow-up, but with less anatomic detail; modern digital VCUG has narrowed the radiation gap. DMSA is best for pyelonephritis and scarring. Routine cystoscopy is not part of modern work-up; uroflowmetry is valuable because reflux is dynamic. Urodynamics help in suspected secondary reflux (sedation alters function).

q: Which statement about renal scintigraphy is TRUE?
o: Acute photopenia always becomes a scar
Resolving photopenia was a resolved scar
Ultrasound is accurate for detecting scars
Photopenia may be scar or renal dysplasia
e: High-grade reflux associates with dysplasia that looks identical to scars; neither DMSA nor ultrasound can separate them. Acute photopenia that persists represents scarring. Greatest risk of post-infection scarring: first year of life.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Renal growth depends only on reflux grade
It is the top cause of severe youth hypertension
Sterile reflux in a high-pressure bladder is benign
Hypertension is unrelated to scar severity
e: Renal growth is affected by associated dysmorphism (about 30%, not caused by reflux), infections, contralateral kidney quality and reflux grade. Book: sterile reflux is benign and reflux matters little without infection when bladder function is normal; high-pressure neurogenic bladders are the exception.

q: Which statement about bladder and bowel dysfunction (BBD) and VUR is TRUE?
o: BBD lowers spontaneous VUR resolution
BBD lowers breakthrough infection rates
BBD has no effect on UTI after surgery
BBD lowers recurrence after endoscopy
e: BBD lowers resolution, raises breakthrough infection, raises recurrence after endoscopic correction and raises post-operative UTI. (The book's answer key marks 'BBD reduces Dx/HA and open success' as false; other studies link BBD to lower endoscopic success.) After stopping prophylaxis, higher-grade VUR and BBD predict recurrent UTI (not uncircumcised boys over 1 year).

q: In complete duplication, the Weigert–Meyer rule places the upper pole ureter:
o: Distal and lateral to the lower pole orifice
Distal and medial to the lower pole orifice
Proximal and medial to the lower pole orifice
Proximal and lateral to the lower pole orifice
e: So the lower pole orifice (lateral, short tunnel) refluxes. About 10% of antireflux surgery involves duplication; use a common-sheath reimplant with one mucosal cuff, because the ureters share a blood supply.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Bladder tone falls, favouring bacteriuria
Upper tract urine volume falls in pregnancy
Bladder tone rises in pregnancy from oedema
Reimplanted women have no extra UTI risk
e: Oedema and hyperaemia lower bladder tone, upper tract volume rises with physiological dilatation. Past reflux, scarring, UTI tendency, hypertension and renal insufficiency add risk; women reimplanted for reflux remain at risk of UTI in pregnancy and need monitoring.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Newborn high-grade VUR resolves more often
About 80% of low-grade reflux resolves
RIVUR: 0.5% drug vs 2% placebo reactions
About half of grade III reflux resolves
e: RIVUR (NEJM 2014) found adverse events in about 2% in both prophylaxis and placebo arms; prophylaxis halved recurrent UTI. Children with grade III–IV reflux, febrile index infection or BBD had more recurrences and seemed to benefit from prophylaxis. Reflux with a paraureteral diverticulum resolves at a rate similar to primary reflux.

q: For a first febrile UTI at 2–24 months, the 2011 AAP guideline recommends:
o: No imaging at all until a second infection
VCUG and ultrasound during the febrile illness
DMSA scan first, then VCUG if it is abnormal
Renal–bladder ultrasound after a culture
e: VCUG only if the ultrasound is abnormal or after a second febrile UTI.

q: What is common to every open antireflux operation?
o: A valve that compresses the ureter
An orifice aimed at the bladder neck
A ureter brought outside the bladder
A tunnel exactly three times the diameter
e: A successful reimplant gives a submucosal tunnel of adequate length (5:1) with good muscular backing. Cohen cross-trigonal reimplant suits small and thick-walled bladders. Contralateral reflux appears in 10–15% after unilateral repair, but prophylactic bilateral reimplantation is not indicated.

q: Early obstruction after reimplantation is managed by:
o: Early reoperation and re-revision
Immediate ureteric stent placement
Observe; divert if symptoms persist
Immediate percutaneous nephrostomy
e: Causes: oedema, subtrigonal bleeding, bladder spasm, mucus, clots, twist or angulation. Most are mild and resolve; symptomatic cases present 1–2 weeks after surgery with pain, nausea and vomiting.

q: Persistent reflux after reimplantation is most often due to:
o: Adequate muscular backing within the tunnel
Too long a submucosal tunnel being made
Missed neuropathic or dysfunctional bladder
Using a common-sheath technique for duplex
e: Besides technical errors (e.g. inadequate muscular backing), failure to identify secondary causes is common. It is not corrected by minor submucosal advancement or reflexive bulking injection.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Needle entry point and placement drive success
All bulking agents work and inject the same
Endoscopy has different indications from open
Endoscopic repair is as durable as open surgery
e: Endoscopic repair is less invasive and less durable. Indications are the same for every approach; the learning curve differs from open surgery (not formally compared).

q: Per the book's answer key, which is NOT associated with higher endoscopic success?
o: Negative intraoperative cystography
Greater surgeon experience
Double HIT technique
Volcano-shaped mound, no hydrodistension
e: The book's explanation is inconsistent (it says none were consistently shown); most other sources link the volcano mound and surgeon experience with success.

q: Which statement about laparoscopic reimplantation is FALSE?
o: Experience is essential to its success
Its success rate is higher than open repair
Cost rises from time and disposables
It gives smaller incisions and faster recovery
e: It needs at least two surgeons, converts an extraperitoneal repair to an intraperitoneal one, and takes longer (shortening with experience); many centres do open reimplants as day cases.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: The whole female urethra is from pelvic UGS
The urachus becomes the median umbilical ligament
The urorectal septum divides the cloaca at 4–6 weeks
Definitive nephrons first make urine at 12 weeks
e: Urine production begins before 12 weeks; the first signs of LUT anomalies may appear around 10 weeks. Allantois and ventral cloaca involute as the bladder descends at 4–5 months.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Transabdominal is better than transvaginal
It normally empties every 15–20 min
Normal 1st-trimester size is ≤12 mm
At 10 weeks 25% of bladders are seen
e: Look carefully before calling a bladder non-visualised. Normal first-trimester bladder is ≤6 mm.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Agenesis occurs in about 1 in 600,000
Bladder agenesis is commoner in males
Exstrophy usually has oligohydramnios
Most exstrophy is diagnosed prenatally
e: Agenesis is commoner in females and compatible with life only if the ureters drain ectopically. Exstrophy usually has normal amniotic fluid and is mostly diagnosed after birth; non-dilated anomalies like exstrophy are among the most severe malformations.

q: Which statement about fetal megacystis is TRUE?
o: It is always from high-grade reflux
Later: fails to empty within 45 min
It always has a dilated posterior urethra
It always means lower tract obstruction
e: In the first trimester it is defined by size (normal ≤6 mm). Persistent megacystis with oligohydramnios suggests LUTO; megacystis resolving before delivery may have no postnatal effects.

q: Which is NOT associated with a better outcome in megacystis?
o: Resolution by 23 weeks
Aneuploidy on gene testing
Initial bladder 12 mm or less
Normal amniotic fluid volume
e: Isolated findings also predict better outcome. Most cases have no genetic diagnosis; when found, trisomy 13 and 18 are commonest, at rates above those expected from maternal age and nuchal translucency.

q: Which statement about megacystis–microcolon–intestinal hypoperistalsis is TRUE?
o: It is usually found by bowel features
No child survives the neonatal period
Thought due to actin muscle defects
It is the commonest cause of megacystis
e: It is rare, usually detected by the bladder finding (may show only prenatal megacystis), and enteric complications cause most morbidity; survival beyond the neonatal period is now documented.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Duplication usually has genital anomalies
Ultrasound equals cystography for diverticula
Congenital diverticula occur in about 20%
Most congenital diverticula need excision
e: Duplication: the urethra may or may not be duplicated, >25% have GI anomalies, and continence is hard to predict. Congenital diverticula: about 1.7%, mostly through a hiatus with mucosa only, usually found after symptoms; cystogram is definitive. Connective tissue disorders: multiple diverticula with muscle and mucosa, treat when symptomatic (stasis, infection, stones), recurrence expected. Large acquired diverticula can obstruct.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Urachal SCC is reported in children
Most patent urachi have outlet obstruction
Infected cysts need no later excision
An omphalomesenteric duct can mimic it
e: Urachal adenocarcinoma occurs in adults; incidental remnants may be excised after discussion because of adult malignant potential. Usually found postnatally with umbilical drainage. Infected remnants: antibiotics, then excision; open or minimally invasive surgery both work.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Haemangioma: Klippel–Trenaunay link
Polyps are the commonest bladder mass
Haemangiomas need radical resection
Haemangiomas are usually multiple
e: Haemangiomas are often single, associated with Klippel–Trenaunay or Sturge–Weber, and simple resection can cure. Fibroepithelial polyps are rare and resected endoscopically. Nephrogenic adenoma: a reaction to infection, stones or injury, commoner in adults, 80% recurrence (latency about 4 years), so routine cystoscopy follows.

q: Which statement is TRUE?
o: Eosinophilic: steroids, antihistamines
Eosinophilic usually progresses in toddlers
Cystitis cystica is commoner in boys
Cystitis cystica is treated with steroids
e: Eosinophilic cystitis is commoner in boys, often self-limited in young children, has no typical appearance and needs biopsy. Cystitis cystica is commoner in girls, can mimic tumour, and is treated with long-term antibiotic prophylaxis. Cyclophosphamide cystitis: give mesna simultaneously; oral pentosan polysulfate shows promise.
